transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-10-26
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Wong (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Crestline HoML), Greg Alvarez (Crestline Infra), Liam O'Connor (Crestline CTO)
Shared artifacts: https://redwood.infra/poc/crestline/latency-deck.pdf, benchmark spreadsheet (link shared in chat)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be fuzzy):
- Reviewed TTFT runs and streaming tradeoffs; saw improvement with streaming + small prompt trims; kernel selection and quantization still under evaluation.
- Decided to run targeted TTFT benchmark with streaming and trimmed prompts, SE to share kernel logs.
- Customer to provide real seq-length distribution for final tuning and cost estimates.

Topics:
- TTFT (time to first token) and streaming impact
- Sequence length distribution and batching behavior
- Kernel choices (flash attention vs fused kernels, Triton vs custom CUDA)
- Quantization and CPU fallback for tails
- Next steps and pricing for Dedicated pool

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia P: hey everyone, thanks for joining, im gonna kick us off. we have 42 minutes, focus on ttft numbers and the streaming experiment results, then next steps.
[00:18] Maya T: thanks, yeah excited. we ran the 1st pass on your streaming build last week, saw some gains but a few weird spikes at p99.
[00:30] Ethan W: cool, can you remind us which model variant you used? was that the quantized 4-bit or the fp16?
[00:36] Maya T: we used the q4_k64 build, i think you call it q4-k64 in the sheet, and streaming flag on. sequences were mostly 256 avg, 95th at 760, 99th at 1,200.
[00:50] Greg A: yeah those long tails are real for us, spikes align with end-of-day batch jobs.
[00:57] Ethan W: ok that explains the p99. so the numbers we saw in the shared sheet: baseline hosted run ttft median ~320ms, p95 ~420ms, p99 ~920ms; with streaming + trimmed prompts median dropped to ~120ms, p95 210ms, p99 560ms.
[01:18] Liam O: those are promising, but we need consistent p99 under 600ms for interactive product. any localization issues?
[01:25] Sofia P: yeah the goal is p99 <600ms for the pilot, target throughput 60 rps. right now we're close but seeing kernel-related jitter.
[01:34] Maya T: quick question, are you using flash attention or fused kernels? our infra folks saw a note about triton kernels in the logs and thought maybe that was the issue.
[01:45] Ethan W: good call. for the streaming run we used the Triton fuse path for attention on the dedicated test nodes. we also tried the asyncronous KV cache optimization, but there might be some contention under tail cases. logs attached show a couple of CUDA context stalls.
[02:03] Greg A: yeah i saw those, some calls showed context switch delays, looked like when seq > 1024 we hit a fallback to CPU path briefly.
[02:12] Ethan W: that's likely the quantization plus kernel mismatch. when a sequence crosses a threshold our runtime chooses a safer kernel (cpu fallback) which spikes latency. we can set a strict kernel pin to avoid fallbacks for the pilot, at the cost of slightly higher avg cost.
[02:28] Maya T: how feasible is pinning kernels? we worry about stability though.
[02:33] Ethan W: it's straightforward to pin to the flash-attn kernel for the common sequence lengths up to 1024; for >1024 we can use a prioritized queue and route those to a different pool or allow slightly higher latency. basically smart routing by seq length.
[02:47] Liam O: route by seq length sounds good. what about ttft impacts when streaming is enabled? some of our prompts are heavy system messages.
[02:55] Ethan W: streaming improves ttft because it starts sending tokens as soon as the first chunk is available. but heavy system prompts increase the initial compile/kernelload cost. trimming system prompts and using prefix caching reduces that. in our trimmed run we saw ttft improve from 320ms to 120ms.
[03:13] Maya T: we did try prefix caching for a common 40-token prefix, but not at the request-level yet, we need guidance on invalidation.
[03:22] Sofia P: we'll share a short doc on prefix cache invalidation patterns. Ethan, add that to action items.
[03:27] Ethan W: noted.
[03:30] [00:03:30] -- short crosstalk as Greg posts the traffic trace link --
[03:42] Greg A: sharing now, the trace link has 7 days with histogram and percentiles. note that seq 512-768 is a big chunk during peak.
[03:50] Ethan W: perfect that'll help us set bundling and batch windows. on kernel choices, we've been testing two options: flash-attn (custom CUDA kernels) and Triton-fused kernels. Flash-attn tends to be lower latency at the cost of higher memory behavior; Triton is more stable for mixed quantization.
[04:10] Maya T: do you see any correctness/regression in outputs switching kernels? we cant afford hallucination differences.
[04:17] Ethan W: good concern. we ran an apples-to-apples QA set across kernels; outputs were consistent for core tasks. minor tokenization differences sometimes appear for edge cases, we flagged those. we can run the full QA suite you provided.
[04:30] Liam O: cost impact? pinning flash-attn will raise cost?
[04:34] Ethan W: small bump per-token but reduces p99 penalties which are costlier if you run retries or extra routing. Our recommendation: pin flash-attn up to 1024 seq, route >1024 to dedicated larger instances or allow degraded latency. also enable streaming and prefix cache; combined we saw median cost down ~12% in our bench but better latency.
[04:56] Maya T: you mentioned kernel logs earlier, can you share the exact log lines so our infra team can map?
[05:02] Ethan W: yes, i'll export the kernel selection trace and include the flags: kernel=flash_attn_v2, fallback=cpu_path, triton_fuse=true. watch for 'KV cache miss' entries, sometimes transcriber shows that as K V cahce.
[05:18] Greg A: haha yes the transcript had that. ok please share.
[05:22] [00:05:22] -- brief silence while file is uploaded --
[05:45] Sofia P: let's talk about streaming window size; we saw different behavior for 16-token vs 32-token chunk sizes. Ethan, which did you bake into the bench?
[05:55] Ethan W: we ran with a 16-token micro-batch for lower latency; 32-token raises throughput but increases ttft slightly. for your interactive flows 16 is safer.
[06:07] Maya T: if we go 16-token and prefix cache, will we still hit the compile cost each cold start?
[06:13] Ethan W: cold starts trigger model compile; we recommend warm lanes or pre-warm for peak hours. warmup endpoints can be scheduled. compile cost is mostly one-time per node unless kernels change.
[06:25] Liam O: whats the devops burden for pre-warming? Greg?
[06:29] Greg A: we can add a small cron job to ping endpoints during peak, not hard. we just need the endpoint list.
[06:35] Sofia P: we will supply recommended warmup scripts.
[06:38] Maya T: another note on quantization: we saw tiny token-level quality deltas when switching to q4_k64; is there a recommended fallback if quality dips at 99th?
[06:49] Ethan W: yes, we suggest a hybrid profile: use 4-bit for most tokens but allow an fp16 hotpath for critical generation segments, or run a QA filter that forces fp16 for flagged prompts. this keeps cost low while preserving critical quality.
[07:05] Liam O: sounds reasonable. cost estimates on dedicated sizing?
[07:09] Sofia P: i'll get updated pricing but rough number for a dedicated pool meeting 60 rps with headroom is X per month, i'll drop exact figures in the SOW.
[07:17] Greg A: can you also include egress and storage for prefix cache?
[07:21] Sofia P: yes will include notes on storage and cache retention policies.
[07:25] [00:07:25] -- Ethan shares a small chart comparing kernel p99s --
[07:40] Ethan W: looking at p99 by kernel: flash-attn pinned = 540ms, triton-fuse = 680ms, fallback cpu path = 1.8s. you can see the big hit when fallback happens.
[07:53] Maya T: that matches our spikes. so action is avoid fallback.
[07:57] Ethan W: yes avoid or route those requests separately. also batching window matters; too aggressive batching increases wait for TTFT. we tuned batch window to 8ms for these runs.
[08:11] Liam O: whats the impact of batching on costs?
[08:14] Ethan W: batching reduces per-token compute and reduces unit cost, but hurts first-token latency. with streaming and prefix cache you regain much of the ttft gains while still batching behind the scenes.
[08:28] Greg A: what about SSO and security for dedicated? we need SOC2 artifacts again.
[08:33] Sofia P: yes we'll re-send SOC2 and network diagrams; dedicated includes VPC peering and KMS integration for keys.
[08:41] Maya T: do you support HSM?
[08:43] Sofia P: yes HSM/KMS via our private offering; we'll note that in the SOW.
[08:49] [00:08:49] -- brief cross talk about scheduling next bench run --
[09:05] Ethan W: proposed bench plan: 1) run TTFT microbench with streaming on and off for seq percentiles you provided; 2) run kernel-pin profile (flash-attn up to 1024) and measure p50/p95/p99; 3) run hybrid quant profile with fp16 hotpath for QA prompts.
[09:22] Maya T: ok do you need any infra changes from our side?
[09:25] Ethan W: we need the traffic trace (you have that), and ability to route a small sample to the dedicated test pool. also logs and permission to read kernel traces. minimal network setup.
[09:36] Greg A: we can carve out a test CIDR for you this week.
[09:40] Sofia P: great. i'll follow up on SOW and pricing.
[09:44] Liam O: timeline? we want pilot performance locked in within two weeks ideally.
[09:48] Sofia P: plan is bench by 10/29, review 11/02, and finalize SOW by 11/09.
[09:55] [00:09:55] -- short pause, some side channel chatting --
[10:12] Maya T: a couple of nitty things: tokenization differences you mentioned, can you run the QA suite with our tokenizer exactly?
[10:18] Ethan W: yes, please attach the tokenizer and we'll run it. also send us a small set of critical prompts.
[10:24] Maya T: will do.
[10:27] Sofia P: ok going to recap.
[10:29] Recap (auto):
- Run TTFT benchmark with streaming + 16-token chunk, prefix cache, and flash-attn pinned up to 1024 (Ethan, due 2027-10-29).
